items.title: The 'Indian Renaissance' — Context & Character
items.body:
## In one line

In the 1800s a group of educated Indians began fighting harmful customs (like widow-burning and child marriage) and rigid religion — an awakening so important it is nicknamed the 'Indian Renaissance'.

## The story

Picture Indian society in the early 19th century weighed down by cruel customs: **Sati** (a widow burned on her husband's funeral pyre), **child marriage**, **female infanticide** (killing baby girls), **untouchability** and a rigid caste system, all defended in the name of religion.

Then two things changed the mood. First, **Western education** and **liberal ideas** (the equality and liberty slogans of the French and American Revolutions) reached Indians through new English schools. Second, the British openly criticised Indian customs, which stung educated Indians into asking: why do we tolerate these evils ourselves? The result was a wave of reformers who attacked the customs from *within* Indian religion, not by abandoning it.

Their work had two sides that always go together. One side was **religious reform** — removing idol worship, superstition and the priests' monopoly, and going back to the "pure" original scriptures. The other side was **social reform** — ending the evils against women and lower castes and spreading education and equality.

## Why it matters / why it is asked

This is the "umbrella" note: prelims asks for the *causes* and *overall character* (a favourite trap is the false claim that reformers avoided social evils), and Mains uses the "Indian Renaissance" idea as the frame for a full essay.

## Picture it

```
Triggers                     Two-sided reform
Western education   ----->   Religious: no idols, back to scripture
Liberal/revolution ideas     Social:   women + caste uplift, education
Colonial critique            = 'INDIAN RENAISSANCE' -> feeds nationalism
```

## Terms explained

- **Sati** — the custom of burning a widow alive on her dead husband's funeral pyre; banned in 1829.
- **Female infanticide** — the killing of newborn girls.
- **Untouchability** — treating certain lower-caste people as 'polluting' and barring them from temples, wells and schools.
- **Indian Renaissance** — the name given to this 19th-century reawakening of rational thought and cultural pride ("renaissance" means rebirth).
- **Monotheism** — belief in one God (preached by the Brahmo Samaj against idol worship).

## Don't confuse

- Reformers did **not** only touch religion — they directly attacked **social** evils (Sati, child marriage). A statement saying they "avoided social evils" is false.
- **Reformist** movements (change old customs) differ from **revivalist** ones (restore a glorious past); many bodies, like the Arya Samaj, were partly both.

## Remember it

Hook: **"Rebirth with two hands"** — one hand cleans up religion (no idols, back to scripture), the other cleans up society (women and caste). Both together = Indian Renaissance.

## TL;DR

- Reform targeted Sati, child marriage, female infanticide, untouchability and caste rigidity.
- Stimuli were Western education, liberal ideas and revolutionary influences plus a colonial critique.
- Movements had a religious wing (anti-idolatry, back-to-scripture) and a social wing (women/caste uplift).
- The reform era is called the 'Indian Renaissance' and helped seed Indian nationalism.
keyPoints: Reform targeted Sati, child marriage, female infanticide, untouchability and caste rigidity.
Stimuli were Western education, liberal ideas and revolutionary influences plus a colonial critique.
Movements had a religious wing (anti-idolatry, back-to-scripture) and a social wing (women/caste uplift).
The reform era is called the 'Indian Renaissance' and helped seed Indian nationalism.

items.title: Brahmo Samaj Lineage & Young Bengal
items.body:
## In one line

This note traces the Brahmo Samaj — the first big reform body, started by Raja Ram Mohan Roy in 1828 — through its two later splits, plus the radical student group called Young Bengal.

## The story

The reform movement really began in Bengal with **Raja Ram Mohan Roy**, often called the **father of the Indian Renaissance**. In **1828** he founded the **Brahmo Samaj**, which preached **one God** (monotheism) and rejected idol worship, caste and superstition. His greatest victory was persuading the British to ban Sati through **Regulation XVII of 1829**.

After his death the Samaj passed through two changes. **Debendranath Tagore** revived it in **1842** as the **Adi Brahmo Samaj**, giving it steady organisation. Later a younger, more radical leader, **Keshab Chandra Sen**, broke away in **1866** to form the **Brahmo Samaj of India**, pushing harder against caste and preaching one universal religion for all.

Alongside the Brahmos, a fiery group of college students in Calcutta formed the **Young Bengal Movement** under their teacher **Henry Louis Vivian Derozio** at Hindu College. Inspired by the French Revolution, they preached pure **rationalism and free thought**, mocked superstition and backed women's education.

## Why it matters / why it is asked

The leader-body-year chain (Roy 1828 → Tagore 1842 → Sen 1866) is a classic matching/statement question, and Derozio's name is a frequent single-answer item.

## Picture it

| Leader | Body | Year | Thrust |
|---|---|---|---|
| Raja Ram Mohan Roy | Brahmo Samaj | 1828 | Monotheism; abolition of Sati (1829) |
| Debendranath Tagore | Adi Brahmo Samaj | 1842 | Rational study of Indian traditions |
| Keshab Chandra Sen | Brahmo Samaj of India | 1866 | Caste abolition; universal religion |

## Terms explained

- **Brahmo Samaj** — "society of worshippers of the one God"; a reform body against idolatry and caste.
- **Regulation XVII of 1829** — the law under Governor-General William Bentinck that made Sati a crime.
- **Monotheism** — belief in a single God.
- **Young Bengal** — the name for Derozio's radical rationalist students at Hindu College, Calcutta.

## Don't confuse

- Three different bodies with similar names: **Brahmo Samaj (1828, Roy)**, **Adi Brahmo Samaj (1842, Tagore)**, **Brahmo Samaj of India (1866, Sen)**. Keep the years attached.
- **Ram Mohan Roy** founded the Brahmo Samaj; **Dayananda** founded the *Arya* Samaj — a very common swap.

## Remember it

Hook: **"Roy-Tagore-Sen = 28-42-66"** for the three Brahmo stages; **"Derozio = daring youth"** for Young Bengal.

## TL;DR

- Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj (1828); Sati was banned by Regulation XVII of 1829.
- Debendranath Tagore founded the Adi Brahmo Samaj (1842).
- Keshab Chandra Sen founded the Brahmo Samaj of India (1866), stressing caste abolition and universal religion.
- The Young Bengal Movement under Derozio preached rationalism and free thought inspired by the French Revolution.
keyPoints: Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj (1828); Sati was banned by Regulation XVII of 1829.
Debendranath Tagore founded the Adi Brahmo Samaj (1842).
Keshab Chandra Sen founded the Brahmo Samaj of India (1866), stressing caste abolition and universal religion.
The Young Bengal Movement under Derozio preached rationalism and free thought inspired by the French Revolution.

items.title: Arya Samaj, Prarthana Samaj & Ramakrishna Mission
items.body:
## In one line

Three more big reform bodies: the Arya Samaj (north India, 'back to the Vedas'), the Prarthana Samaj (western India), and the Ramakrishna Mission (Bengal, service + spirituality).

## The story

As reform spread beyond Bengal, three important bodies appeared. In north India, **Dayananda Saraswati** founded the **Arya Samaj in 1875** with the slogan **'Go back to the Vedas'** — he said the Vedas were the pure source and attacked idol worship, caste rigidity and empty rituals. He also started the **Shuddhi** movement to bring converts back into Hinduism, and his key book was *Satyarth Prakash*.

In western India, the **Prarthana Samaj (1867)**, with **M.G. Ranade** as its guiding figure, acted as the Bombay cousin of the Brahmo Samaj, working for caste equality, widow remarriage, women's education and Hindu-Muslim harmony.

In Bengal, **Swami Vivekananda**, the chief disciple of the saint **Ramakrishna Paramahamsa**, founded the **Ramakrishna Mission in 1897**. Unlike purely religious bodies, it combined **practical social service and education** with the philosophy of **Vedanta**. Vivekananda had already made India famous abroad with his address at the **World Parliament of Religions, Chicago, 1893**.

## Why it matters / why it is asked

These three founders and years (Dayananda 1875, Ranade/Prarthana 1867, Vivekananda 1897) are heavily tested in match-the-following, and Vivekananda's 1893 Chicago date is a stand-alone favourite.

## Picture it

```
1867  Prarthana Samaj   - M.G. Ranade (western India)
1875  Arya Samaj        - Dayananda Saraswati ('back to the Vedas', Shuddhi)
1893  Chicago address   - Vivekananda
1897  Ramakrishna Mission- Vivekananda (service + Vedanta)
```

## Terms explained

- **'Back to the Vedas'** — Dayananda's call to treat the ancient Vedas as the true, pure guide and reject later superstitions.
- **Shuddhi** — the Arya Samaj's ceremony to "purify" and reconvert people (back) to Hinduism.
- **Vedanta** — a school of Hindu philosophy based on the Upanishads, stressing the oneness of the self and the divine.
- **Parliament of Religions (1893)** — a world gathering of faiths in Chicago where Vivekananda spoke for Hinduism.

## Don't confuse

- **Arya Samaj (Dayananda, 1875)** vs **Brahmo Samaj (Ram Mohan Roy, 1828)** — different founders, different decades.
- **Prarthana Samaj (1867)** is the western-India body; don't place it in Bengal.

## Remember it

Hook: **"Vedas-Dayananda, Prarthana-Ranade, Ramakrishna-Vivekananda."** Chicago = 1893, Mission = 1897.

## TL;DR

- Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj (1875): 'back to the Vedas', Shuddhi movement, Satyarth Prakash.
- M.G. Ranade co-founded the Prarthana Samaj (1867) for caste equality and widow remarriage.
- Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission (1897) for social service and Vedanta.
- Vivekananda addressed the World Parliament of Religions at Chicago in 1893.
keyPoints: Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj (1875): 'back to the Vedas', Shuddhi movement, Satyarth Prakash.
M.G. Ranade co-founded the Prarthana Samaj (1867) for caste equality and widow remarriage.
Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission (1897) for social service and Vedanta.
Vivekananda addressed the World Parliament of Religions at Chicago in 1893.

items.title: Women's Reform & Community Reform (Muslim, Parsi, Sikh)
items.body:
## In one line

Reform was not only Hindu or only about religion: this note covers the drive to help women (through laws and schools) and the parallel reform among Muslims, Parsis and Sikhs.

## The story

The worst-treated group was women, so reformers pushed for both **laws** and **schools**. **Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar** fought for widows and won the **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act of 1856**, and also opposed child marriage and polygamy. Later, **Behramji Malabari's** campaign against child marriage produced the **Age of Consent Act of 1891**. On the ground, **Savitribai Phule** became one of India's first female teachers and fought female infanticide, while **Pandita Ramabai** (Sharda Sadan) and **Annie Besant** built institutions for women's education.

Reform also spread across religious communities. Among **Muslims**, **Sir Syed Ahmad Khan's Aligarh Movement** promoted modern Western education (MAO College), while the **Deoband** school stressed traditional Islamic learning. Among **Parsis**, the **Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha (1851)**, linked to **Dadabhai Naoroji**, reformed customs. Among **Sikhs**, the **Singh Sabha** and later **Akali** movement worked to reform Gurudwaras.

## Why it matters / why it is asked

The women's laws (1856 and 1891) with their reformer-names, and the community-wise matching (Aligarh-Muslim, Rahnumai-Parsi, Singh Sabha-Sikh), are both repeat question types.

## Picture it

| Movement | Community | Leader |
|---|---|---|
| Aligarh Movement (MAO College) | Muslims (modern education) | Sir Syed Ahmad Khan |
| Deoband School | Muslims (orthodox education) | Deoband ulema |
| Ahmadiyya (1889) | Muslims (universal brotherhood) | Mirza Ghulam Ahmad |
| Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha (1851) | Parsis | Dadabhai Naoroji |
| Singh Sabha / Akali | Sikhs (Gurudwara reform) | Singh Sabha leaders |

## Terms explained

- **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (1856)** — the law allowing Hindu widows to remarry legally.
- **Age of Consent Act (1891)** — the law raising the minimum age at which a girl could be married/cohabit (to 12).
- **MAO College** — the Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental College founded by Sir Syed; it later became Aligarh Muslim University.
- **Ulema** — Muslim religious scholars (the Deoband school was run by the ulema).
- **Gurudwara reform** — the Sikh movement to free their shrines from corrupt control.

## Don't confuse

- **Aligarh (Sir Syed)** = *modern* Western education; **Deoband** = *orthodox* traditional education. They are opposites, often paired as a trap.
- **Vidyasagar** = Widows' Remarriage Act 1856; **Malabari** = Age of Consent Act 1891. Keep the pairs straight.

## Remember it

Hook: **"1856 widow (Vidyasagar), 1891 consent (Malabari)"** for women's laws; **"Aligarh modern, Deoband orthodox"** for the Muslim split.

## TL;DR

- Vidyasagar drove the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (1856); Malabari the Age of Consent Act (1891).
- Savitribai Phule, Pandita Ramabai and Annie Besant advanced women's education.
- Aligarh Movement (Sir Syed Ahmad Khan) promoted modern Muslim education; Deoband stressed orthodox education.
- Ahmadiyya (Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, 1889), Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha (Parsi, Naoroji) and Singh Sabha/Akali (Sikh) reformed their communities.
keyPoints: Vidyasagar drove the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (1856); Malabari the Age of Consent Act (1891).
Savitribai Phule, Pandita Ramabai and Annie Besant advanced women's education.
Aligarh Movement (Sir Syed Ahmad Khan) promoted modern Muslim education; Deoband stressed orthodox education.
Ahmadiyya (Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, 1889), Rahnumai Mazdayasnan Sabha (Parsi, Naoroji) and Singh Sabha/Akali (Sikh) reformed their communities.

items.title: Anti-Caste & Self-Respect Movements
items.body:
## In one line

This note covers the reformers who attacked the caste system head-on — Phule in Maharashtra, Narayana Guru in Kerala, and the Justice Party and Periyar in the south.

## The story

While the Brahmo and Arya Samajes reformed religion, a bolder set of leaders attacked **caste itself**, speaking for the lower castes who were kept out of temples, schools and dignity.

In Maharashtra, **Jyotirao Phule** founded the **Satyashodhak Samaj (1873)** ('society of truth-seekers'), opposed Brahmin dominance, wrote the famous book ***Gulamgiri*** ('Slavery'), and opened schools for lower castes and girls. In Kerala, **Sree Narayana Guru** gave the great message **'One caste, one religion, one God for mankind'**; in **1888** he boldly consecrated a temple at **Aravippuram** open to all castes, and in **1903** the **SNDP** was formed to uplift the Ezhava community.

In the south (Madras), the **Justice Party (1916)** challenged Brahmin dominance in jobs and education, and its agitation led to a **1930 Government Order granting reservations**. Then **Periyar E.V. Ramaswami** launched the rationalist **Self-Respect Movement (1925)**, running the journal ***Kudi Arasu***, demanding full dignity and equality for non-Brahmins.

## Why it matters / why it is asked

Movement-year-leader matching (Satyashodhak 1873, Aravippuram 1888, Justice Party 1916, Self-Respect 1925) is a near-certain question, and the SNDP slogan is a stand-alone item.

## Picture it

| Movement | Region | Year | Leader |
|---|---|---|---|
| Satyashodhak Samaj | Maharashtra | 1873 | Jyotirao Phule |
| Aravippuram / SNDP | Kerala | 1888 / 1903 | Sree Narayana Guru |
| Justice Party | Madras | 1916 | T.M. Nair, P. Tyagaraja Chetti |
| Self-Respect Movement | Tamil Nadu | 1925 | Periyar E.V. Ramaswami |
| Depressed Classes (Mahars) | Maharashtra | 1924 | B.R. Ambedkar |

## Terms explained

- **Satyashodhak Samaj** — Phule's "truth-seekers' society" working against caste oppression.
- **Gulamgiri** — Phule's 1873 book comparing caste oppression to slavery.
- **SNDP** — Sri Narayana Dharma Paripalana Yogam (1903), the body uplifting the Ezhavas in Kerala.
- **Aravippuram** — the place where Narayana Guru installed a Shiva idol in 1888 to show lower castes could worship too.
- **Self-Respect Movement** — Periyar's rationalist movement for the dignity and equality of non-Brahmins.

## Don't confuse

- **Phule's Satyashodhak Samaj (1873, Maharashtra)** is different from **Periyar's Self-Respect Movement (1925, Tamil Nadu)** — different leaders, regions and decades.
- **Aravippuram (1888)** is the temple event; **SNDP (1903)** is the later organisation — both under Narayana Guru.

## Remember it

Hook: **"Phule seeks truth (1873), Guru opens the temple (1888), Periyar seeks self-respect (1925)."**

## TL;DR

- Jyotirao Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) and wrote Gulamgiri against caste oppression.
- Sree Narayana Guru led the Aravippuram (1888) / SNDP (1903) movement: 'One caste, one religion, one God'.
- The Justice Party (Madras, 1916) opposed Brahmin dominance; its stir led to a 1930 reservation order.
- Periyar's Self-Respect Movement (Tamil Nadu, 1925) was rationalist; his journal was Kudi Arasu.
keyPoints: Jyotirao Phule founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) and wrote Gulamgiri against caste oppression.
Sree Narayana Guru led the Aravippuram (1888) / SNDP (1903) movement: 'One caste, one religion, one God'.
The Justice Party (Madras, 1916) opposed Brahmin dominance; its stir led to a 1930 reservation order.
Periyar's Self-Respect Movement (Tamil Nadu, 1925) was rationalist; his journal was Kudi Arasu.

items.title: Reform in Andhra — Veeresalingam, Gurajada, Naidu, Gidugu
items.body:
## In one line

This is the key AP-focused note: four Telugu reformers who modernised both Andhra society and the Telugu language in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

## The story

The reform spirit reached the Telugu country strongly, and its towering figure was **Kandukuri Veeresalingam (1848–1919)**, called the **father of the Telugu Renaissance**. Inspired by Brahmo Samaj ideals, he organised the **first widow remarriage in the Telugu region at Rajahmundry in 1881**, fought **dowry, child marriage and the nautch (devadasi) system**, and opened **schools for girls**. He also used the pen: he edited the reformist journal ***Vivekavardhini*** and wrote ***Rajasekhara Charitramu***, an early Telugu social novel.

His contemporaries widened the awakening. **Gurajada Apparao (1862–1915)** wrote ***Kanyasulkam*** (1892), the first modern Telugu play, mocking the custom of selling young girls in marriage; he also championed everyday **spoken (vaaduka) Telugu** and wrote the patriotic poem *Desamunu Preminchumanna* ('Love your country'). **Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu (1862–1939)**, a leading **Brahmo Samaj** reformer and educationist, led the **anti-nautch** and **social-purity/temperance** campaigns. **Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy (1863–1940)** fought for **Vyavaharika Bhasha (spoken Telugu)** against the old classical **Grandhika** style and studied the **Savara tribal language** — his birthday, **29 August, is now Telugu Language Day**.

## Why it matters / why it is asked

This is prime APPSC material: who did the first widow remarriage, who wrote *Kanyasulkam*, whose birthday is Telugu Language Day — all common single-answer and matching questions, and the core of the AP Mains answer.

## Picture it

| Reformer | Years | Key contribution |
|---|---|---|
| Kandukuri Veeresalingam | 1848–1919 | First Telugu widow remarriage (1881); Vivekavardhini; Rajasekhara Charitramu |
| Gurajada Apparao | 1862–1915 | Kanyasulkam (1892); spoken Telugu; Desamunu Preminchumanna |
| Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu | 1862–1939 | Brahmo Samaj; anti-nautch & social-purity/temperance |
| Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy | 1863–1940 | Vyavaharika Bhasha movement; Savara study; Telugu Language Day (29 Aug) |

## Terms explained

- **Nautch / devadasi system** — the practice of dedicating girls to temples as dancers; reformers campaigned to end it ("anti-nautch").
- **Vivekavardhini** — Veeresalingam's reformist Telugu journal.
- **Vyavaharika Bhasha** — everyday *spoken* Telugu (what Gidugu promoted for writing).
- **Grandhika** — the old, classical, bookish Telugu style that Gidugu opposed.
- **Kanyasulkam** — literally "bride-price"; the title of Gurajada's 1892 play attacking that custom.

## Don't confuse

- **Veeresalingam** did the *reform work and the first widow remarriage*; **Gurajada** wrote *Kanyasulkam* — do not swap them.
- **Gidugu** (spoken-Telugu movement, Telugu Language Day) is different from **Gurajada** (playwright), though both backed spoken Telugu.
- Some digests loosely list Veeresalingam under 'Veda Samaj' (a Madras body linked to Chembeti Sridharalu Naidu); his own work centred on the Rajahmundry reform associations and Brahmo ideals.

## Remember it

Hook: **"Veeresalingam reforms, Gurajada writes the play, Naidu fights the nautch, Gidugu frees the language."** Telugu Language Day = Gidugu's birthday, 29 August.

## TL;DR

- Kandukuri Veeresalingam — father of the Telugu Renaissance; first Telugu-region widow remarriage (Rajahmundry, 1881); journal Vivekavardhini; novel Rajasekhara Charitramu.
- Gurajada Apparao wrote Kanyasulkam (1892) against bride-price/child marriage and championed spoken Telugu; poem Desamunu Preminchumanna.
- Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu led the Brahmo Samaj in Andhra and the anti-nautch and social-purity/temperance movements.
- Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy led the Vyavaharika Bhasha (spoken-Telugu) movement and studied Savara; 29 August is Telugu Language Day.
keyPoints: Kandukuri Veeresalingam — father of the Telugu Renaissance; first Telugu-region widow remarriage (Rajahmundry, 1881); journal Vivekavardhini; novel Rajasekhara Charitramu.
Gurajada Apparao wrote Kanyasulkam (1892) against bride-price/child marriage and championed spoken Telugu; poem Desamunu Preminchumanna.
Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu led the Brahmo Samaj in Andhra and the anti-nautch and social-purity/temperance movements.
Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy led the Vyavaharika Bhasha (spoken-Telugu) movement and studied Savara; 29 August is Telugu Language Day.

items.title: Reform Journals, Legal Cases, Schools & Theosophy (PYQ set)
items.body:
## In one line

A set of smaller but frequently-asked facts — the first Dalit journal, a famous women's court case, an early girls' school, key reform-era books and the Theosophical Society.

## The story

Reform also happened through **journals, courts and schools**. **Gopal Baba Walangkar** published ***Vital-Vidhvansak*** in **1888**, regarded as the **first monthly for the 'untouchables'/Depressed Classes** — an early voice of Dalit assertion. **Keshab Chandra Sen** (of the Brahmo Samaj of India) founded the **Indian Reform Association (1870)** and the **Church of the New Dispensation (Nava Vidhan, 1880)**.

In the courts, the **Rakhmabai case (1884)** became famous when a woman, married as a child, refused to live with her husband; the case turned on **restitution of conjugal rights** and stirred debate on **women's education** and the **age of consent**, feeding the **Age of Consent Act of 1891**. Earlier, the **Bethune School (Calcutta, 1849)**, founded by **J.E.D. Bethune** with **Vidyasagar** as its secretary, had become a pioneer of girls' education.

Two more exam staples: the order of reform-era **books**, and the **Theosophical Society** — founded by **Blavatsky and Olcott** in **New York (1875)**, with its Indian headquarters moving to **Adyar, Madras (1882)**, later led by **Annie Besant**.

## Why it matters / why it is asked

These are the exact facts UPSC/APPSC have asked as single-answer and chronology questions (Vital-Vidhvansak, Rakhmabai, Neel Darpan–Arya Samaj–Anandamath order, Theosophical Society).

## Picture it

| Work | Author | Year |
|---|---|---|
| Neel Darpan (indigo planters' oppression) | Dinabandhu Mitra | 1860 |
| Arya Samaj founded | Dayananda Saraswati | 1875 |
| Anandamath (Vande Mataram) | Bankim Chandra Chatterjee | 1882 |

## Terms explained

- **Vital-Vidhvansak** — "destroyer of ritual pollution"; Walangkar's 1888 journal for the Depressed Classes.
- **Restitution of conjugal rights** — a court order forcing a spouse to live with the other; the core issue in the Rakhmabai case.
- **Age of Consent Act (1891)** — raised the minimum marriage/cohabitation age for girls to 12.
- **Nava Vidhan** — the "New Dispensation", Keshab Chandra Sen's universal faith (1880).
- **Theosophical Society** — a body blending Western occultism with Hindu-Buddhist philosophy; HQ at Adyar, Madras.

## Don't confuse

- The first Depressed-Classes journal was **Walangkar's Vital-Vidhvansak (1888)** — *not* Ambedkar's later Mooknayak (1920). Ambedkar is the usual trap option.
- Chronology trap: **Neel Darpan (1860) comes before the Arya Samaj (1875), which comes before Anandamath (1882).**

## Remember it

Hook: **"60-75-82"** = Neel Darpan, Arya Samaj, Anandamath. **"Walangkar was first"** for the Dalit journal.

## TL;DR

- Gopal Baba Walangkar's Vital-Vidhvansak (1888) = first monthly for the Depressed Classes/'untouchables'.
- Keshab Chandra Sen: Indian Reform Association (1870) & Church of the New Dispensation (Nava Vidhan, 1880); Calcutta Unitarian Committee link.
- Rakhmabai case (1884) touched women's education, age of consent & restitution of conjugal rights; fed the Age of Consent Act 1891.
- Bethune School (1849, J.E.D. Bethune) — Vidyasagar its secretary; female education.
- Chronology: Neel Darpan (1860) < Arya Samaj (1875) < Anandamath (1882).
- Theosophical Society: Blavatsky & Olcott (New York 1875); HQ Adyar, Madras (1882); later Annie Besant.

Keshab Chandra Sen: Indian Reform Association (1870) & Church of the New Dispensation (Nava Vidhan, 1880); Calcutta Unitarian Committee link.
Rakhmabai case (1884) touched women's education, age of consent & restitution of conjugal rights; fed the Age of Consent Act 1891.
Bethune School (1849, J.E.D. Bethune) — Vidyasagar its secretary; female education.
Chronology: Neel Darpan (1860) < Arya Samaj (1875) < Anandamath (1882).
Theosophical Society: Blavatsky & Olcott (New York 1875); HQ Adyar, Madras (1882); later Annie Besant.

items.title: For Mains — Socio-Religious Reform Movements
items.body:
## In one line

For Mains (GS Paper-II, clauses M2-4 and M2-4b), reform is asked as analysis: its character, its contribution to social awakening and nationalism, its limits, and the strong Andhra/Telugu angle.

## The story

Mains answers must argue, not list. Use the dimension table to decide the demand of the question, then build intro–body–conclusion around 3–4 dimensions, always closing with a balanced verdict and an AP example.

| Dimension | What to write | Sharp point to quote |
|---|---|---|
| **Causes/context** | Social evils + Western education + colonial critique | Sati, child marriage, caste rigidity |
| **Character** | Twin religious + social reform; reformist vs revivalist | Brahmo Samaj (1828) vs Arya Samaj (1875) |
| **Contribution** | Women, caste, education, legislation | Sati ban 1829; Widows' Remarriage 1856; Age of Consent 1891 |
| **Link to nationalism** | Collective identity & cultural pride | Vivekananda at Chicago (1893) |
| **Limitations** | Elite/urban, revivalist, sometimes communal | Internal splits in the Brahmo Samaj |
| **AP angle** | Telugu social + linguistic renaissance | Veeresalingam, Gurajada, Gidugu |

**Data / laws / people to quote:** (1) Regulation XVII of 1829 (Sati ban); (2) Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act 1856; (3) Age of Consent Act 1891; (4) Rakhmabai case 1884; (5) Dayananda's *Satyarth Prakash*; (6) Vivekananda's 1893 Chicago address; (7) Phule's *Gulamgiri* (1873).

**AP angle (use this to score):** the Telugu country had its own renaissance — **Kandukuri Veeresalingam** (first Telugu widow remarriage, Rajahmundry 1881; *Vivekavardhini*), **Gurajada Apparao** (*Kanyasulkam*, 1892), **Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu** (anti-nautch/temperance) and **Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy** (spoken-Telugu movement; Telugu Language Day, 29 August). This links the all-India movement to Andhra and almost always wins marks.

## Why it matters / why it is asked

M2-4 lists socio-religious reforms with nationalism, and M2-4b lists Phule, Narayana Guru and Periyar — so the examiner expects you to connect reform to both the national awakening and the anti-caste/self-respect currents.

## Terms explained

- **Reformist vs revivalist** — reformist movements change old customs; revivalist ones restore an idealised past. A good answer notes many bodies were a mix.
- **Social awakening** — the spread of rational, equal-rights thinking across society.

## Don't confuse

- "Was it a renaissance?" wants a *balanced* verdict (great awakening, but elite/urban and partly revivalist), not blanket praise.

## Use in answers

- **Example to cite:** Veeresalingam's 1881 Rajahmundry widow remarriage as the AP mirror of Vidyasagar's 1856 Act.
- **Quote:** Sree Narayana Guru's **'One caste, one religion, one God for mankind'** to anchor the anti-caste dimension.
- **Diagram idea:** a two-column balance sheet — "Achievements vs Limitations" — to structure the body and show evaluation.

## TL;DR

- Treat reform as analysis: context → character → contribution → link to nationalism → limitations.
- Anchor with laws and texts: Sati ban 1829, Widows' Remarriage 1856, Age of Consent 1891, Gulamgiri 1873, Satyarth Prakash.
- Always add the AP angle: Veeresalingam, Gurajada, Naidu, Gidugu (Telugu social + linguistic renaissance).
- Close with a balanced verdict: a genuine 'Indian Renaissance', yet elite/urban and partly revivalist.

Link to nationalism via collective identity and cultural pride (e.g. Vivekananda at Chicago, 1893).
AP angle: Veeresalingam (1881), Gurajada (Kanyasulkam 1892), Naidu (anti-nautch), Gidugu (spoken Telugu, Telugu Language Day).
